newsitem.title: UK: UK's Blair wins surprising newspaper converts.
newsitem.headline: UK's Blair wins surprising newspaper converts.

text.p: Labour party leader Tony Blair must wait a little longer to see whether he has won the hearts and minds of the British people. But he's already won some surprising converts among the partisan press.

As British newspapers cast their editorial votes on the May 1 election, revamped Labour is winning endorsements that must have been beyond its wildest dreams after an ignominous fourth straight defeat at the polls in 1992.
Britain's two best-selling tabloids -- The Sun and the News of the World -- have ditched the ruling Conservatives to declare Blair the "man for the new millennium".
It was all very different five years ago when The Sun persecuted then Labour leader Neil Kinnock and trumpeted after the Conservatives clinched a surprise victory; "It's The Sun Wot Won It."

The Financial Times, bible of the business community, has also come out for Labour, which after 18 years in opposition has ditched its socialist traditions and transformed itself into a centrist party.
Blair, tipped by opinion polls to win a landslide victory on Thursday but desperate to avoid seeming complacent, has played down his delight at finally winning over some of Labour's fiercest critics.
"I am very happy to have endorsements from whatever quarter from the media. That is jolly good and we are very pleased about it," Blair said on Tuesday.
"But the endorsement I really want is the endorsement from the British people on May 1 and that is the one that we intend paying most attention to," he added.

Some political anlaysts link the Sun's change of heart to the commercial interests of its Australian-born owner Rupert Murdoch, whose media empire includes three other British newspapers and a satellite television station.
Blair made a point of courting Murdoch, with whose papers Labour once refused all contact.

But The Times -- also from the Murdoch stable -- surprised political commentators on Tuesday by refraining from endorsing any of the three main parties. It urged readers to vote for individual candidates opposed to further European integration.

And Murdoch's fourth British national newspaper, the Sunday Times, stuck with the Conservatives, although its backing was less than enthusiastic. "Only the Tories, warts and all, offer the prospect of lasting improvement," it said.
Likewise the Mail on Sunday, which urged readers to give John Major's Conservatives another chance.
London's Evening Standard, a strident past supporter of the Conservatives, switched to Labour citing the democratic argument for change.
"Mr Blair understands that the British electorate today wants a change of leadership, not a change of economic direction," the Evening Standard said.

The ability of the media to swing votes at such a late stage is however in doubt. Political analysts and journalists pore over newspaper comment columns with enthusiasm but they probably do more to reflect public opinion than to influence it.
"Campaign shift is very modest -- only about two or three percent. The contribution of editorials is miniscule really," said Professor Tom Nossiter of the London School of Economics..
"The way in which papers go is partly a function of changes in society... and has a lot to do with commercial imperatives," he added.
